content: 1. Specific taxation applies a uniform tax rate per unit of ethanol, regardless of the perceived quality or value of the alcoholic beverage. This is represented as a horizontal line in tax rate comparisons. 2. Ad valorem taxation imposes a tax based on the value of the perceived qualities per unit of ethanol, leading to a steeper slope in tax rate comparisons. This system incentivizes producers to lower the quality of their products to reduce tax burdens. 3. Mixed Specific and Ad Valorem (MSA) taxation combines elements of both specific and ad valorem taxation. When MSA taxation leans toward specific taxation, its effects resemble those of specific taxation, with a less steep slope in tax rate comparisons. Conversely, when MSA taxation favors ad valorem taxation, its effects are closer to ad valorem taxation, with a steeper slope. 4. Specific taxation encourages producers to improve the quality of their products, leading to higher prices and reduced alcohol consumption. In contrast, ad valorem taxation incentivizes producers to downgrade product quality, resulting in lower prices and increased alcohol consumption. 5. MSA taxation promotes the production of medium-quality alcoholic beverages, as it balances the attributes of both specific and ad valorem taxation systems. 6. Ad valorem with specific floor (ASF) taxation ensures that the tax rate for any alcoholic beverage is never lower than the specific tax rate. For lower-quality beverages, the ASF tax rate equals the specific tax rate, while for higher-quality beverages, the ASF tax rate equals the ad valorem tax rate. 7. ASF taxation reduces alcohol consumption and related harms, prevents drinking initiation by heavily taxing low-ethanol content beverages, and increases tax revenue. However, it may discourage the production of high-quality, expensive alcoholic beverages, reducing product variety in this category. 8. Minimum pricing per unit of ethanol sets a price floor for alcoholic beverages, preventing sales below a designated price. This policy increases the price of low-cost alcoholic beverages, reducing their consumption and associated harms, particularly among heavy drinkers and low-income populations. 9. Minimum pricing, when combined with taxation, generates tax revenue while ensuring that the difference between the minimum price and the taxed price benefits alcohol companies. However, its ability to prevent drinking initiation is uncertain, as low-ethanol content beverages are typically expensive and unaffected by minimum pricing. 10. Governments may adopt differential tax methods and rates to discourage the consumption of specific alcoholic beverages, such as heavy spirits, or to align the price of spirits with other alcoholic beverages due to their lower production costs. 11. Uniform taxation methods and rates may be justified when alcohol consumption produces similar consequences across beverage types. However, differential taxation can lead to substitution effects, where consumers shift to less-taxed beverages, potentially undermining public health goals. 12. Tax rate assessments can be measured using two indicators: the tax as a percentage of retail price (TPP) and the tax per unit of ethanol (TPU). TPP reflects the tax burden relative to the beverage's retail price, while TPU measures the tax burden per unit of ethanol. Both indicators are essential for cross-country comparisons of alcohol excise tax rates. 13. Specific taxation reduces alcohol consumption and related harms while increasing tax revenue. However, it may encourage drinking initiation among young people, as they often consume low-ethanol content beverages that are less heavily taxed under this system. 14. Ad valorem taxation increases tax revenue but also raises total alcohol consumption and drinking initiation, as it promotes the availability of low-cost alcoholic beverages. 15. Unitary taxation promotes inexpensive, high-ethanol content beverages and a wide variety of product qualities. However, it is unlikely to reduce alcohol consumption or prevent drinking initiation, though it does increase tax revenue. 16. MSA taxation is less effective than uniform specific taxation in controlling alcohol consumption, as it promotes lower-cost alcoholic beverages. However, it may prevent drinking initiation by encouraging the production of medium-alcohol content beverages. 17. ASF taxation is effective in reducing alcohol-related harms, preventing drinking initiation, and increasing tax revenue. However, it may generate lower tax revenues from expensive beverages if these products are more elastic compared to inexpensive alcoholic beverages. 18. The literature has extensively analyzed the attributes of specific and ad valorem taxation, but further empirical studies are needed to evaluate the theoretical assessments of unitary, MSA, and ASF taxation systems.
